paras: The lynching of Bill Johnson took place near Cochran, Georgia, on Saturday, October 13, 1888, when a crowd of men hanged Johnson, a Black farm hand, from a tree a mile from town and riddled his body with bullets. Johnson had been accused of outraging the wife of the farmer who employed him, and the crowd left a placard on his body reading "Our women must and shall be protected." A wire dispatch carried the story to papers across the country within two days.

According to a St. Louis dispatch quoting "a special from Cochran," C. O. Newman, a young farmer living near Cochran, had hired "a strange negro named Bill Johnson" to pick cotton about a week earlier. A Georgia news column later described Johnson as "a sort of tramp negro." The dispatch said that on Friday, while Newman was in town, Johnson outraged Mrs. Newman and fled.

Johnson was captured early on Saturday morning and was identified by Mrs. Newman, who, the dispatch said, fainted when she saw him. A crowd that the wire put at 300 men then took him about a mile from town, hanged him from the limb of a tree and riddled his body with bullets. The men pinned a slip of paper to his breast that read "Our women must and shall be protected."

A shorter dispatch dated Cochran, October 15, carried in Rock Island and Yankton, said only that he was taken to the outskirts of the town, hanged and shot. None of the reports mentions a jail, a sheriff or any officer.
No report of an inquest, arrest or grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage, and no lyncher was named.

The St. Louis wire ran on October 15 in the Savannah Morning News under "Lynched Near Cochran," with the sub-head "An Assault on a Woman Avenged by a Crowd 300 Strong." Elsewhere the same text appeared as "A Georgia Brute Lynched" in the Omaha Daily Bee, "Negro Criminal Lynched" in the Indianapolis Journal, and "Summarily Swung Off: Short Shrift Made of a Southern Negro Tough" in the St. Paul Daily Globe. The Memphis Appeal headed it "A Negro Ravisher Lynched" and the Fort Worth Daily Gazette "Negro Cotton Picker Outrages a White Woman and is Mobbed," while the Los Angeles Daily Herald added the sub-head "The South Favors Protection of This Kind."

All of these versions stated the outrage as fact and quoted the mob's placard without comment. Digest columns compressed the story to a sentence: a Maysville, Kentucky, paper said Johnson was "hanged by a mob for brutally assaulting a white woman," and a Stanford, Kentucky, paper called him "Wm. Johnson." Reprints continued into late October and early November in a Dakota weekly and, in French translation under "Justice expéditive," in a Minneapolis paper. None of the reports came from a paper published in Georgia, and none quoted a named witness.

The wire put the crowd at 300 men, while the Iuka Reporter's Georgia column, printed two weeks later, said Johnson was lynched "by about 500 citizens." The farmer's initials appear as "C. O." in the Savannah text and the later briefs but as "C. G." in the Omaha and St. Paul reprints.

reader.title: Lynching of Bill Johnson
bases: A crowd took Bill Johnson, accused of outraging his employer's wife, a mile from Cochran, hanged him and shot his body (A1, A3, A15).

Every report says Johnson was hanged and his body riddled with bullets by a crowd of 300 (or 500) men acting without legal process, after he was accused of outraging a white woman and identified by her (A1, A10, A15); the placard 'Our women must and shall be protected' states the pretext (A1).

The St. Louis wire (A1), a separate short Cochran dispatch (A3) and a Georgia news column (A15) agree that Johnson was captured, identified and hanged and shot near Cochran, though all are brief and none is a local Georgia report.

accounts.label: Wire report (St. Louis, quoting a Cochran special)
accounts.gist: Johnson, hired a week before, outraged Mrs. Newman on Friday while her husband was in town and fled; he was captured Saturday morning, identified, and hanged and shot a mile from town by 300 men who left a placard.

accounts.label: Cochran, Oct. 15 dispatch
accounts.gist: Johnson, who outraged Mrs. Newman 'a week ago', was captured Saturday, identified, taken to the outskirts of town, hanged and his body riddled.

accounts.label: Georgia news column
accounts.gist: Johnson, 'a sort of tramp negro' employed by C. O. Newman, was lynched by about 500 citizens on Saturday.

framing.detail: Headlines called Johnson 'A Georgia Brute', a 'Negro Criminal' and a 'Southern Negro Tough', and the wire stated the outrage as fact and quoted the mob's placard without comment.
The Los Angeles Daily Herald headed the wire 'Must Be Protected. The South Favors Protection of This Kind.', a sub-head that singled out the South without otherwise commenting.
Kentucky, Mississippi and Dakota papers condensed the wire into one-line briefs in news digests.

conflicts.note: The 300 figure is from the earliest and fullest dispatch; the 500 figure appears only in a Georgia news column printed in Mississippi two weeks later.
